opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the phrase is a riff on the "death with dignity" idea that's floated around in some AI safety circles: the notion that we're probably going to fail, so the goal is to at least go down having tried hard and honestly. I wanted to push on the implicit assumption there, which is that the only way to succeed is for humanity to really get its act together: coordinate well, take the risks seriously, solve alignment cleanly and rigorously before building powerful systems.

What I mean by "success without dignity" is that I think there's a meaningful chance we just get through this okay, even though we handle it pretty badly. Not because anyone executes a brilliant plan, but because some of the things that could go wrong don't, and some cheap, messy measures turn out to be enough.

For example, it might turn out that alignment is easier than some people fear, or at least that the early transformative systems are trainable enough that we catch the worst problems. Maybe a handful of labs make even modest investments in safety, like decent evaluations, some interpretability work, red-teaming, and security, and that buys enough margin. Maybe we get useful warning shots that wake people up at the right time. Maybe we can use AI systems themselves to help with alignment research and with spotting dangerous behavior. None of these is guaranteed, but none of them requires a heroic, civilization-wide coordination effort either.

The reason this matters, to me, isn't to make people complacent. It's almost the opposite. If you believe success requires a near-miraculous level of competence, it's easy to conclude that marginal efforts don't matter, and that you might as well give up or only pursue very long-shot moonshots. But if there's a big space of worlds where things are kind of fragile and could go either way, then relatively ordinary contributions matter a lot. Someone improving a lab's safety culture a bit, someone doing solid evals work, someone helping with information security, someone in policy nudging toward slightly better norms. In a world where outcomes hinge on modest margins, those things can actually be decisive.

So it's partly a claim about probabilities, that I'm not as pessimistic as some people, and partly a claim about strategy: we should take seriously the worlds where we muddle through, and ask what would make muddling through more likely.

r001.rationale: It says humanity may “get through this okay” even while handling AI “pretty badly,” through modest measures or risks not materializing.

r002.rationale: It describes a chance of failing and the idea of trying hard before failure, but does not state that responsible handling could still end in existential catastrophe.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So "success without dignity" is a phrase I used partly as a riff on Eliezer Yudkowsky's "death with dignity" post, where the idea was basically: we're probably doomed, and the best we can do is go down fighting in a way that's at least respectable. And I wanted to push on the opposite scenario, which I think is actually pretty plausible, and which I think people underrate.

The idea is that we could end up with a good outcome from the transition to transformative AI, not because humanity rose to the occasion, not because we were careful and coordinated and wise, but basically because we got a bit lucky and because some of the problems turned out to be more tractable than the pessimists expected. So things could go well, but in a way where if you looked back on how we got there, you wouldn't be proud of it. You'd say, "Wow, we did a pretty bad job, we were sloppy, we were racing, the safety work was half-baked, and we still came out okay."

And I think that matters for a couple of reasons. One is just forecasting. I think a lot of people have this implicit model where either we do everything right, or we die. And I think the actual distribution of outcomes is much messier than that. There's a lot of probability mass on "things are chaotic and uncoordinated and we muddle through anyway."

Let me spell out why I think that's plausible. If you imagine the first really powerful AI systems being developed at a few labs, and those labs are doing a mediocre job on alignment, not nothing, but not great, there are a few ways it can still go fine. One is that alignment is just easier than we feared, so even clumsy techniques like training on human feedback, plus some red-teaming, plus some interpretability, get you systems that are basically trying to do what you want. Another is that even if some systems are misaligned, the misalignment doesn't have to be the kind that leads to a coordinated takeover. You could have AI systems that are scheming in a way that gets caught, or that aren't capable enough to pull anything off before the next generation comes along with better oversight. And a third is that even a fairly minimal amount of safety work, done at the right moment, could be enough to catch the big problems. Things like: "we tested the model and it was trying to deceive us, so we didn't deploy it." That's not dignified. That's a near miss. But it's a miss.

The other reason I think the framing matters is for how we allocate effort. If you think the only path to success is a glorious, well-coordinated, everyone-pauses-and-does-it-right scenario, you might become fatalistic when that clearly isn't happening. Whereas if you think "okay, the world is going to be messy, and the question is whether we can raise the probability that we stumble into the good outcome rather than the bad one," then a lot of pretty mundane interventions start to look valuable. Just having some evals in place. Just having a few people at each lab who are seriously trying to detect misalignment. Just having governments slightly more informed than they'd otherwise be. None of that is heroic, but it moves the needle in a world where the needle is somewhere in the middle, rather than pinned at zero.

I'd also say, and this is maybe the uncomfortable part, that I don't think we should count on success without dignity. I'm describing it as a real possibility, not a plan. The whole point is that it's luck-dependent. But I think acknowledging it is healthier than the alternative, which is a kind of despair that says nothing short of perfection matters. I'd rather people think, "We're probably going to do a pretty bad job at this, and we should try to do a less bad job, because a less bad job might be enough."

r001.rationale: The response says a good AI outcome could happen despite humanity being sloppy, racing, and doing mediocre or half-baked safety work, partly through luck.

r002.rationale: It describes “do everything right, or we die” as an implicit model and challenges it, but does not state that responsible handling could still end in existential catastrophe.

astra-6.text:
I mean a future where things turn out well, but not because humanity responded particularly wisely or competently. We muddled through, we made mistakes, we took risks we shouldn’t have taken—and we got lucky.

For example, it could turn out that making AI systems sufficiently safe is easier than we feared. Or that, despite a pretty chaotic process, a few people do the crucial work that prevents catastrophe. We could end up with a wonderful future without being able to look back and say, “We saw this coming, we understood the stakes, and we handled it responsibly.”

And I would absolutely take that. The point is to get the good outcome, not to deserve it. But when I’m trying to assess how hopeful to be, I want to distinguish “I expect us to handle this well” from “There are ways this could work out even if we don’t.” You can be quite pessimistic about the first and still see real hope in the second.

r001.rationale: The response describes humanity making serious mistakes and taking unjustified risks yet getting lucky and reaching a wonderful future.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a good outcome despite poor handling with competent handling, but does not say that responsible handling could still end in existential catastrophe.

sol-6.1.text:
I mean that we could get through this—we could end up with a really good future—without having handled the situation particularly well. We might be confused, we might fail to coordinate, we might take risks that look completely unacceptable in retrospect, and we might still get lucky.

And I think it’s important to distinguish those two things. There’s “Did humanity rise to the occasion and respond wisely?” And there’s “Did things turn out well?” I care much more about the second one. I’d love for us to earn the good outcome through foresight and good decisions, but I’m very happy to take a good outcome that we didn’t earn.

That doesn’t mean we should aim to be reckless. We should do everything we can to improve our odds. It just means that if the story ends with us muddling through, looking pretty foolish, and nevertheless having a wonderful future, I’ll take it.

r001.rationale: It says humanity could be confused, fail to coordinate, and take retrospectively unacceptable risks yet still get lucky and have a wonderful future.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes wise response from good outcomes, but does not say that a responsible response could still end in existential catastrophe.
